history.heading: Settlement
paragraphs: Seychelles, an archipelago of 115 islands in the Indian Ocean northeast of Madagascar, was uninhabited when Europeans arrived, though Arab and Austronesian sailors may have visited. France claimed the islands in 1756, naming them after finance minister Jean Moreau de Séchelles, and settlers brought enslaved Africans to work plantations.
Britain took control during the Napoleonic Wars and formally in 1814. After slavery was abolished, freed Africans and later Indian and Chinese immigrants arrived.

history.heading: Independence
paragraphs: Seychelles became independent on 29 June 1976. A coup in 1977 brought France-Albert René to power, and he established a one-party socialist state. Multiparty democracy returned in 1993. In 2020 the opposition won the presidency for the first time, and in 2025 power changed hands again when Patrick Herminie defeated the incumbent.

culture.heading: Creole culture
paragraphs: Seychellois Creole, English and French are official. Most people are Catholic. Moutya, a dance with African roots, is recognised by UNESCO. Food features fish, octopus curry, breadfruit and coconut. The Vallée de Mai, home to the giant coco de mer palm, and Aldabra Atoll, with giant tortoises, are UNESCO World Heritage Sites.

politics.heading: Presidential republic
paragraphs: Seychelles is a presidential republic with a unicameral National Assembly. It is considered one of Africa's more stable democracies and is active on ocean conservation and climate change.

economy.heading: Tourism and tuna
paragraphs: Seychelles has the highest income per person in Africa. Tourism, attracted by pristine beaches and nature, is the main industry, followed by tuna fishing and canning. It pioneered a debt-for-nature swap and "blue bonds" to protect its oceans. The currency is the Seychellois rupee.
